newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--Durable goods, 2-yr note sale.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--Durable goods, 2-yr note sale.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury market gets the April durable goods orders report and $16.5 billion in new supply of two-year notes on Wednesday.
The durable goods orders, due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, are forecast up 1.3 percent for April, reflecting a partial bounceback from a 2.6-percent decline in March.

Economists said orders for defense goods and commercial aircraft could rebound. On the other hand, auto industry strikes crimped vehicle assemblies in April and probably led to lower orders in the auto sector last month, they said.

After a couple of months of weakness in orders for durable goods, a modest rebound in April would not change people's perceptions of the economy, economists said. Certainly the economy slowed in the second quarter from its first quarter growth of about 6.0 percent, economists said. The question is whether the economy will decelerate even more in the second half of the year or continue to grow at a fairly brisk pace. The April durable goods orders data really cannot answer that question, they said.

The market will get one privately collected economic report on Wednesday -- the BTM/Schroders weekly chain store sales index. The index usually is released on Tuesday but was postponed a day due to the Memorial Day holiday on Monday. U.S. chain store sales rose 0.3 percent in the week ended May 17 from the prior week, according to the seasonally adjusted index. A forecast for the week ended May 24 was not available.

Once the durable goods orders data and the weekly store sales data are digested (the latter are officially due at 0900 EDT/1300 GMT but are often in the market before then), the market will position itself for the two-year T-note sale.

The Treasury is scheduled to sell $16.5 billion in two-year notes on Wednesday and $12 billion in five-year notes on Thursday. The bidding deadlines are 1300 EDT/1700 GMT on Wednesday and Thursday, respectively.
Two year notes yielded 6.27 percent in late trade on Tuesday and in when-issued trade, the two-year notes to be sold on Wednesday were yielding 6.31 percent.

Analysts said a key issue would be what yields are appropriate for two-year notes now that the Federal Reserve's May 20 policy meeting has passed without a rate hike -- but in light of the possibility of a future rate hike.

A yield of 6.25 percent, for instance, would scarcely reflect any risk of a future Fed interest-rate tightening, said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc., who believes that "before the year is out, we'll see more tightening from the Fed."

"A two-year yield at 6.25 percent is not cheap, let's put it that way," said Josh Feinman, vice president and global markets economist at Bankers Trust. "People have been pretty complacent about the risk of the Fed tightening. We start to get data for May next week and I suspect they're going to be on the firm side," he said.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond ended at 95 even on Tuesday, down 15/32 to yield 7.03 percent.
Dealers indicated that Federal funds would open at 5-1/2 percent on Wednesday.
